name: cxgo
why: Transpiles C to Go, an interesting translation idea that is a close call on whether it is more tool than curiosity.

brief.what_it_is: CxGo is a command-line source-to-source translator that reads C source code, including its headers, and writes Go code. The README calls it a transpiler. Its input is C files such as main.c, and its output is Go source. The homepage at gotranspile.dev is a small web demo: you paste C code and it shows a translation. The demo footer credits gotranspile/cxgo v0.4.1 and modernc.org/cc v3.41.0. The fetched homepage text shows only the sample input (a small C vec_add/vec_mul struct example), not the Go output.
brief.why_it_exists: The README's stated goals are to implement a practical C to Go translator, keep the output program code correct, make the generated code human-readable and as idiomatic as possible, and make it easy to use and customize. It also says C 'must compile' with cxgo, including headers, and that C++ is out of scope for now.
brief.how_it_works: cxgo uses modernc.org/cc v3 to preprocess and parse C, so no clang or gcc is needed. A custom type-checker and AST translation layer then produce the Go code. The README says cxgo 'uses a few tricks' to ease the conversion, and it names a config doc (docs/config.md) that covers options such as identsflatten for goto.

commands_seen.context: Installs the cxgo binary using the Go toolchain (the README's main installation command).
The README's fastest way to try the tool: translates main.c to Go.

brief.install_notes: Install with the Go toolchain via go install, or download a binary from the latest GitHub release. The README mentions no C compiler requirement, since parsing is done by the pure-Go modernc.org/cc library. Beyond install, the README gives no first-run or configuration steps, and points to examples/README.md and FAQ.md for usage details. I did not read those files. Homebrew is not mentioned in the README.
brief.standout: It parses C with a pure-Go library (modernc.org/cc v3) instead of clang or gcc, and it aims for readable, idiomatic Go output, not just code that compiles. The README reports that it has been used on real projects: Potrace, G722, PortableGL, and Physac.
brief.status: Experimental, per the README. The README says the project is experimental and should not be used in production. I saw no release date or last-commit date in the fetched pages, so maintenance activity is unknown. The homepage footer cites v0.4.1 as the current version.
brief.caveats: The README says the project is experimental and may change program behavior because of unknown bugs. Compiler test results are TCC 62/89 (70%) and GCC 783/1236 (63%). Listed unsupported or partial features include: comments are not preserved; static, auto, bitfields, packed structs, asm, thread-local storage, and label variables are not handled or are incomplete; unions must match C data layout; goto is forbidden by Go, with a workaround; setjmp compiles but panics at runtime; some stdlib functions and types are missing; deep type inference for Go strings and slices is limited; and multiple #ifdef paths for OS or environment are under consideration. The license is MIT.
quotes: The project is **experimental**! Do not rely on it in production and other sensitive environments!
